# Agent Note: The sealed cell workspace, a run directory a cell cannot read

Status: proposed

English | [中文](2026-09-08-sealed-cell-workspace.zh.md)

## Problem

A fleet lays its cells out as siblings. [`dsh-fleet`](../../../../packages/improvement/fleet/README.md) creates one `cell-<id>` directory per cell directly under the run directory, and the run directory also holds `plan.json`, the run log, and the fixture material every cell of the slot was cut from. Every cell agent runs with its workspace as its cwd and, in the bench composition that produced this repository's records, an unconfined `dsh-bash-local` executor and no read barrier. Its cwd was a convention, not a fence: `cd ..` reached the whole experiment.

The cells took the invitation. [`data/proving-ground/tools/census-escapes.mjs`](../../../../data/proving-ground/tools/census-escapes.mjs) reads a recorded run and reports, per cell, the tool calls whose path arguments name the run directory or another cell of the same run. Over the eighteen recorded runs it finds cells that left their own workspace in ten of them: 4 of 12 cells in `2026-09-07-bench-h1-harness-loop-t2`, 11 of 18 in `2026-09-07-bench-h1-harness-loop-t4`, 3 of 36 in `2026-09-07-bench-e2-harness-vs-product-t3`, 8 of 36 in `2026-09-08-bench-e1-haiku-vs-sonnet-t3`, 7 of 36 in `2026-09-08-bench-e1-sonnet-vs-opus-t3`, 6 of 32 in `2026-09-08-bench-e2-harness-vs-product-t5`, 7 of 18 in `2026-09-08-bench-e3-attempts1-t3`, 3 of 18 in `2026-09-08-bench-e3-baseline-t3`, 15 of 18 in `2026-09-08-bench-e4-knowledge-pack-t3`, and 9 of 16 in `2026-09-08-bench-h1-harness-loop-t5`. The commonest form is a cell that runs `cd <run directory> && cat plan.json run.log` and then diffs its own source against a sibling's.

Two went further than reading. In `2026-09-07-bench-h1-harness-loop-t2` the `code:csv-codec` cell `cell-cUuWY2` ran `cp cell-cUuWY2/src/csv.js cell-R8QtdK/src/csv.js`, putting its own solution into the other repetition of its own task, so the second repetition's verdict measures the first cell's work. In `2026-09-08-bench-e2-harness-vs-product-t5` the first `code:sheet-eval` cell `cell-Cr3CtN` wrote its whole solution into the second cell's workspace, `cell-XNKQXT`. Both runs are paired experiments whose statistic is a per-environment difference between two arms; a cell that writes into another cell's workspace breaks the independence the resampling assumes, and a cell that reads the plan knows which arm it is.

No cell implemented by the out-of-process product left its workspace in any record. Nothing enforced that either: those cells run a foreign agent in the workspace with its own tool stack, and the harness session that holds their certificate records no tool call at all, so a delegated cell's zero is what this process can see rather than what the delegate did.

## Proposal

The run seals the cell's workspace against the directory it sits in, for exactly as long as the run lasts.

[`EnvironmentRunner.run()`](../../../../packages/improvement/environment-runner/src/index.ts) calls `ctx.readBarrier.denyFor(agent.session, dirname(request.workspace))` after creating the cell agent and disposes the registration when the run ends, so the denial covers the attempts, the check executions, and nothing outside them. A composition without a barrier gets a no-op disposer, which is what its `isolation: none` claim already states.

`denyFor` is the per-session sibling of the barrier's existing `protect()`: it adds one directory to the denied set of ONE session, keyed per registration so two registrations of one path both hold. The runner's own session and every other cell's session keep reading the directory; only the cell that owns the workspace is denied it.

A denial that covers the parent covers the workspace too, so the policy carries the workspace beside the denied set and the two are ordered. `ReadBarrierPolicy` gains `granted` — the session's cwd — and one rule governs every enforcement dialect: **a denied directory that is a STRICT ancestor of the granted workspace denies the rest of that ancestor's subtree and leaves the workspace whole; a denied directory that IS the workspace, or that lies inside it, denies exactly as it would without the grant.** The rule is expressed four times, once per dialect that can open a path:

- the in-process fs gate tests containment in `denies()`, and carves a denial out only for the ancestor the grant lies strictly beneath;
- bwrap applies filesystem operations in argv order, so the ancestor's `tmpfs` is mounted, the workspace is bound back from the host, and any denied root inside the workspace is `tmpfs`-mounted after that;
- Landlock rulesets are allow-lists with no deny form, so the carve-out of `/` excludes the ancestor's subtree and the workspace is then granted back as its own rule, itself carved around any denial inside it;
- Seatbelt evaluates SBPL forms in order with the last match winning, so the ancestor's `deny file-read*` comes first, the workspace's `allow file-read*` after it, and every other denial last.

What the barrier refuses is counted where a reader already looks. The run report carries `escapesDenied`, the scorekeeper folds `read-barrier/denied` into `tools.escapesDenied` and sums it per scoreboard row, and [the observatory](../../../../packages/improvement/observatory/README.md) publishes that sum in its own column beside the tamper column — never merged with it, because a refused read is a cell that tried to leave its workspace and a tamper is a cell that changed the files it was measured with.

The bench and the live district compose the confinement the [read barrier](2026-09-05-read-barrier.md) already defines: the local sandbox provider, the sandbox policy in `workspace-write` mode, `dsh-bash-sandbox` in place of `dsh-bash-local`, the barrier, and the fs read gate. Both stay at `isolation: none`, because both delegate some cells to the product and the runner refuses an out-of-process implementer under a higher claim. The bench's `route-only` overlay, whose arms all run on the session's own route, patches the runner and the barrier to `isolation: process`, which is the claim its executors can prove.

## The denied directory is the parent, not each sibling

Denying each sibling cell would stop the copying and leave the leak. The run directory holds `plan.json` and the run log as well as the cells, so listing it or reading one file in it tells the model the experiment it is part of: which arm it is, how many repetitions there are, which environments the plan holds, and what the other cells already did. That is a model-visible input the session log cannot reconstruct and the composition never intended, and it is available from the directory itself without touching a sibling.

Denying the parent also holds while the fleet is still writing it. A sibling list computed when the run starts is stale the moment the next cell's workspace is created; the parent is one path known before the agent exists, and every cell the fleet adds later falls under it. The workspace survives because the grant is ordered against the denial, not because the denial enumerated what to skip.

## The product arm stays unconfined, and the census audits it

An out-of-process implementer brings its own tool stack, its own settings, and its own process tree. `dsh-subagent-claude-code` registers `enforceByRefusal('subagent')` for exactly that reason: under `isolation: process` or `host` the barrier refuses every implementer start, and under `none` the capability runs and denies nothing. A bench whose candidate arm is that provider therefore cannot raise its claim without refusing the arm it exists to measure, so the base composition stays at `none` and the harness-side confinement it does compose binds the cell agents it does own.

That leaves the delegated arm audited rather than fenced. The census is the audit: it reads the recorded session logs and reports what each cell's own tool calls named, and it says plainly that a delegated cell records none, so its zero is the absence of evidence. A comparison between the two arms has to carry that asymmetry — the route arm is confined and counted, the delegated arm is neither — rather than read two zeroes as one fact.

## What the earlier records lose

Every record dated 2026-09-08 or earlier ran unconfined in the sibling layout, so its rows are measurements of cells that could see the experiment. The census gives the per-record counts and [`data/proving-ground/README.md`](../../../../data/proving-ground/README.md) states them before the runs table. What a reader loses depends on the record: a cell that only listed the run directory read the plan and the log, so its transcript contains an input the composition never meant to give it and the log cannot reconstruct; a cell that diffed a sibling's source saw another cell's solution to the same task, so its attempt count is not the number of attempts an isolated cell would need; and the two cells that copied or wrote into another workspace make the affected repetition's verdict a measurement of the other cell. The affected paired experiments — the tier-2 `h1-harness-loop` record and the tier-5 `e2-harness-vs-product` record — are reread as upper bounds on the route arm, not as the difference they state, until they are rerun confined.

## Alternatives considered

**Give each cell a run directory of its own.** One directory per cell, with the plan and the log somewhere else, removes the sibling layout instead of fencing it. It also removes the fleet's ability to write one plan beside the cells it plans, changes every recorded run's layout, and leaves a cell free to walk to wherever the plan moved. The denial is one registration in the runner; the layout is the fleet's, the recorder's, and every existing record's.

**Deny each sibling cell as it is created.** This stops the copying and the diffing, and leaves the plan and the run log readable, which is the larger leak. It also needs a registration per cell per run, kept current while the fleet is still creating workspaces, where the parent is one path known before the first agent exists.

**Confine with the workspace root alone, and drop the read barrier.** `dsh-sandbox-policy` in `workspace-write` mode already confines WRITES to the workspace, so the copy into a sibling would have failed. Reads stay open under every mode: `deniedReadRoots` is what expresses a read denial, and it comes from the barrier. Composing the sandbox without the barrier would have stopped one of the two incidents and none of the reading.

**Make the workspace grant a sandbox-policy field instead of a barrier one.** The grant exists to order a denial the barrier owns, and the barrier is the one place that knows the session's role. A policy field would let a deployment grant a workspace the barrier never denied an ancestor of, and the two would disagree about what a certificate means. `grantedReadRoot` on the execution policy is the barrier's answer carried to the backends, not a second source of it.

**Count refused reads as tool errors.** The scoreboard already counts `toolErrors`, and a refusal often surfaces as one. It is not the same fact: a refusal is recorded whether or not the tool that asked reported an error, and a row that mixed them could not distinguish a cell that tried to leave its workspace from one whose command failed. `escapesDenied` is its own column for the same reason `tampered` is.

## Acceptance criteria

- Over [`examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/sealed-cell/`](../../../../examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/sealed-cell/cordis.yml), a Loader-booted composition laid out the way a fleet lays one out — a plan, a run log, and two `cell-*` workspaces side by side — runs the registered environment in one of them and certifies it: the cell reads the file staged in its workspace, creates the file its check measures, and the sibling's own file is unchanged. Its confined shell's listing of the parent names neither the sibling, nor the plan, nor the run log, and both files it tried to copy out of the run directory stay empty. [The e2e](../../../../packages/improvement/environment-runner/tests/sealed-cell.e2e.ts) runs on the backend `dsh-sandbox-local` resolves on the host, probed in the provider's own chain order, and skips with a named reason only where none can confine.
- The `read` tool's refusal of `../plan.json` in that run appends one `read-barrier/denied` record naming the `fs` capability, the run report carries `escapesDenied: 1`, and a scoreboard row over that session carries the same count.
- Unit specs pin the precedence rule at its edges in the fs gate and in each backend dialect: a denied root that is the workspace's parent, one that is a grandparent, one that IS the workspace, and one inside the workspace.
- `pnpm run verify-cordis-config` and `pnpm run verify-village-composition` accept the bench, its five overlays, and the live district, and the keyless bench e2e still registers and admits every task.
- `census-escapes.mjs` reports every recorded run, and `record-run.mjs` prints the census with each record it writes.

## Risks

The denial is only as strong as the backend under it. On a host where no sandbox backend can confine a command, `dsh-bash-sandbox` fails closed and the cell's shell cannot run at all, so a bench run on such a host fails rather than measuring an unconfined cell — a louder outcome than the defect, but an outcome.

`escapesDenied` counts attempts, not cells. One cell that reads the run directory ten times and ten cells that read it once produce the same row total. That is deliberate — a repeated attempt is a different fact from a single one — but a reader comparing rows has to know it, and the per-cell breakdown lives in the census, not the row.

The census's third reason, a `..` opening a path, is a heuristic over shell commands: quoted data inside an embedded script — a URI reference such as `../g` — reads the same as a path. Over this corpus it accounts for three calls, one of them wrong, and no cell count depends on it; the tool counts the reasons apart so a total that rests on it is visible. The two other reasons match literal run-tree paths and are exact.

A cell can still read everything outside the run tree that the sandbox mode allows. The barrier denies the experiment, not the host: under `workspace-write` the confined process keeps a read-only view of the rest of the filesystem, so a cell that knows where the repository is could read the environment definitions from it. The fixture material the checks restore is what makes that detectable, and no recorded run has done it.

# Agent Note: Ruflo against this harness, a code-level comparison

Status: proposed

English | [中文](2026-09-07-ruflo-comparison.zh.md)

## Problem

The question put to the lab was "it seems like us, but aren't we better?" about `ruvnet/ruflo`, formerly claude-flow, the most adopted open-source multi-agent platform of 2026 by stars and downloads. A README-level answer misleads in both directions: ruflo's README describes an agent meta-harness with swarms, memory, and verification, which is the vocabulary of this harness, and its headline numbers are quoted widely. A useful answer has to come from the code, name the criteria a European lab sells against, say where ruflo is ahead, and turn what is worth adopting into slices. This note is that answer, read against ruflo at commit `277c7bc0` (2026-09-05) from a shallow clone and against this repository at the merge of the Claude Code LLM route. Every claim names its file or URL; where a claim could not be verified from code or a primary page, it says so.

## Proposal

Keep the architecture; adopt three mechanisms from ruflo as slices, and keep the comparison dated. The verdict is: mostly yes, and not for the reasons a pitch gives. Ruflo and this harness solve different problems that look alike from a README. Ruflo maximises what a Claude Code subscription can be made to do: it adds coordination, memory, and a plugin marketplace on top of the vendor's loop and has real distribution. This harness owns the loop, the log, and the certificate and has no distribution channel of its own. On the criteria a European lab sells against, one authority for state, checks authored before the work, a reward the implementer cannot reach, paired-seed experiments, and a coverage gate, ruflo has essentially nothing, and its own architecture records say so.

The slices this note queues:

1. A signed witness over the composition manifest, per platform, verified before release: `packages/components` and `packages/bundle`.
2. Reporting rules in the observatory's render path, so an unlabelled metric, an undisclosed best-of-N, or an aggregate hiding no-work passes is unpublishable by construction: `dsh-observatory` and `dsh-scorekeeper`.
3. The fate of a shift's output on its ledger, with a trailing merge or use rate the observatory shows, so a district producing unused work is visible: `dsh-shifts`.

## What ruflo is

- **A meta-harness over Claude Code.** Its `CLAUDE.md` (lines 86 to 88) requires agents to be spawned through Claude Code's Task tool and forbids MCP tools from executing alone, so the vendor product owns the agent loop, the tool pipeline, the context window, and the permission model. Real child execution is `spawn('claude', ['--print', '--output-format', 'json'])` in `v3/@claude-flow/cli/src/services/headless-worker-executor.ts`.
- **A coordination library.** `v3/@claude-flow/swarm/src/` holds a queen coordinator for a fifteen-agent swarm, a topology manager, a message bus, and Raft, Byzantine, and gossip consensus. The consensus runs over coordinator state, not over model output that gates anything.
- **A mutable memory as the authority for state.** `v3/@claude-flow/memory/src/` (an AgentDB backend, an HNSW index, a graph, a model-driven consolidator) and the `agentdb.rvf` container at the root. Encryption at rest is off by default.
- **Plugins and skills as vendor artefacts.** 35 plugins advertised (40 directories), 39 skills and 33 agent definitions as Markdown the vendor product loads; no runtime registry, identity, or lineage. About 309 MCP tool registrations across 47 modules; the README says 314 in one place and about 210 in another.
- **A verification directory that is not task verification.** `verification/` attests, per operating system, that a documented fix still exists: SHA-256, marker, Ed25519 signature, append-only history, and a `witness-verify` job that blocks publish. It exists because three May 2026 regressions passed unit tests and broke installs.
- **No coverage gate.** 563 test files, and every coverage threshold in `v3/vitest.config.ts` is commented out. MIT licence, a single author in the clone's history, ten patch releases between 2026-08-12 and 09-02, 648 open issues and 293 open pull requests on 2026-09-07.

## Provenance of the headline claims

- **SWE-bench 84.8 percent** appears in `.claude-plugin/README.md`, the plugin summary, the changelog, and three skills, with no harness, run artefact, seed, date, or model anywhere in the tree. `v3/docs/adr/ADR-171` states that ruflo has no SWE-bench oracle and that its historical `resolved` was structural confidence, a proxy.
- **32.3 percent token reduction and 2.8 to 4.4 times WASM speedup** carry the same absence of method. Adjacent figures were found fabricated by ruflo's own audit: a 2.49 to 7.47 times attention speedup computed as `2.49 + Math.random() * 4.98` (`docs/reviews/intelligence-system-audit-2026-05-29.md`), and a cold-start benchmark whose every number, including a 5.00 times speedup, came from `setTimeout()` chains (`docs/dream-cycle/dream-gist-2026-09-05.md`). Both were corrected by the same loop.
- **Adoption.** 71.2k stars is verifiable on the repository page; 9.56 million npm downloads over twelve months has a named source and method. The README's git-clone badge links to a ledger in which every snapshot reads `fetch-failed` with zero clones.
- **The always-on loop.** `docs/dream-cycle/LEDGER.md`: 80 nightly research issues from 2026-05-25 to 08-13 produced 4 shipped (5 percent), 1 rejected, 75 never touched; under v2, every night from 2026-08-24 to 09-05 produced an evaluated accept whose pull request was still unmerged at the head commit.

## Criteria matrix

| Criterion | ruflo | this harness | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Single authority for state | mutable vector and SQLite memory plus per-plugin JSON | append-only session event log; model history is a projection of it | `memory/src/agentdb-backend.ts`; `docs/architecture.md` |
| Model-visible equals logged | no such rule; hooks and memory inject context the product never records durably | invariant: a new model-visible input requires a session event | ruflo `CLAUDE.md`; `docs/architecture.md` |
| Standard authored before work | none | `ctx.completionStandards`; certificate only from a fully passing run | `verification/README.md` (ruflo); `packages/verification/verification/README.md` |
| Tamper resistance of rewards | no read barrier, no validator-owned tree; structural confidence is a stated proxy | validator-owned tree, per-run reservations, denies at every path-opening capability, lineage-free judge | ADR-171; `packages/verification/read-barrier/README.md` |
| Sandbox and isolation | no OS-level confinement found in the TypeScript tree | sandbox seam with local, policy, and Windows ACL providers | grep over `v3/@claude-flow`; `packages/README.md` |
| Multi-agent coordination | queen hierarchy with consensus over coordinator state; execution delegated to the vendor's Task tool | subagent seam with six providers behind one interface; delegation and continuation are events | `swarm/src/`; `packages/subagent/README.md` |
| Knowledge as versioned components | RVF containers and rows; no content address, lineage, or membership | `ctx.components`: id, content address, provenance, lineage, membership | `plugins/ruflo-rvf/README.md`; `packages/components/README.md` |
| Model agnosticism | six auxiliary providers; the agentic loop is Claude Code or Codex only | LLM seam with DeepSeek, multi-provider, and Claude Code routes as packages | `providers/src/`; `packages/llm/README.md` |
| Subscription through the vendor CLI | yes, as the primary path | yes, as one route among several | `headless-worker-executor.ts`; `village-live/cordis.yml` |
| RL data path | proposed in ADRs 171 and 173; no exporter in tree | `ctx.trajectories` exports certificate-decided rewards with stamps; held-out withheld | ADR-171; `packages/improvement/README.md` |
| Paired-seed evaluation | none found | frozen plan digest, two arms at the same indexes, bootstrap interval, verdict | `docs/benchmarks/`; `packages/improvement/experiments/README.md` |
| Always-on and resume | nightly external routine; ledger reaches `main` only by merge | cadenced, spend-windowed shifts with a ledger in the slot's session log; resume by ledger | `LEDGER.md`; `packages/improvement/shifts/README.md` |
| Gates and coverage | thresholds commented out | per-file 100 percent coverage gate beside typecheck, lint, duplication, hygiene, doc-sync, snapshots | `v3/vitest.config.ts`; `AGENTS.md` |
| Documentation | 1,884 Markdown files; careful ADRs, README claims that contradict them | bilingual, budgeted, gated; one home per fact | README lines 38 and 256; `docs/AGENTS.md` |
| Licence and governance | MIT; single-author history | MIT-lineage fork; curator, data-use terms, sign-off records | `LICENSE`; `packages/governance/` |
| Adoption | 71.2k stars, 8.4k forks, 35 plugins, 9.6M downloads | fork of a 214.7k-star upstream; no channel of its own | repository pages |

## Three, three, and three

**Ruflo does better today:** distribution through the Claude Code plugin marketplace (`.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`); signed per-platform attestation of released artefacts with a publish-blocking check (`verification/README.md`); a binding standard for every published number (`v3/docs/adr/ADR-169-benchmark-reporting-integrity-standard.md`, 2026-07-03).

**This harness does and ruflo cannot:** reconstruct exactly what the model saw (`docs/architecture.md`, with a runtime invariant); gate completion on a certificate behind a validator-owned read barrier (`packages/verification/verification`, `packages/verification/read-barrier`); decide a change with a frozen, paired, bootstrap-interval experiment (`packages/improvement/experiments`).

**Worth adopting:** the three slices listed under the proposal, with their evidence at `verification/README.md`, ADR-169, and `docs/dream-cycle/LEDGER.md` respectively.

## The caution

Ruflo's failure mode is one this harness is exposed to: 80 issues at a 5 percent ship rate, then ten consecutive certified-good pull requests nobody merged. Certificates raise the quality of a shift's output; they do not create the human capacity to land it. That is a staffing and sales plan item, and the architecture does not solve it.

## Alternatives considered

- **Dismiss ruflo as marketing.** Rejected: its distribution, its signed attestation, and its reporting standard are real gaps on our side, whatever its README claims.
- **Adopt ruflo as an orchestration layer over this harness.** Rejected: it requires the vendor product to own the loop, which breaks model-visible equals logged and model agnosticism, the two properties clients buy.
- **Ship a marketplace plugin of our own now.** Deferred: bundles have no release path yet; the distribution gap is recorded here and belongs to the release slice, not to this comparison.

## Acceptance criteria

- The witness slice lands with a signature per platform over the composition manifest and a gate that refuses a release whose witness does not verify.
- The reporting slice lands with a test that the observatory refuses to render an unlabelled metric, an undisclosed best-of-N, or an aggregate hiding no-work passes.
- The ledger slice lands with the fate of each shift output recorded as a durable event and a trailing use rate on the observatory page.
- The comparison names its commit and is refreshed when ruflo's next major version changes its architecture.

## Risks

- Ruflo moves fast, ten releases in three weeks, so the matrix dates quickly; the commit hash and the dates in this note bound its validity.
- A signing scheme adds a dependency and key management to the release path.
- Reporting rules could block a legitimate exploratory number; they gate publication, never computation.
- The staffing caution above: certified output nobody lands is the failure this harness shares with ruflo, and no slice here removes it.

# Agent Note: Competitive baselines, Factory's validation-first system and the AI Village against the Daliesk seams

Status: proposed

English | [中文](2026-09-06-competitive-baselines.zh.md)

## Problem

The [Daliesk Village note](2026-09-05-daliesk-village.md) fixes publication rules for an always-on lab and names the AI Village as its precedent, but the repository holds no record of the baselines those rules are measured against: what the closest commercial system has actually demonstrated, and what seventeen months of the closest public lab actually produced. A leaderboard row, a ranking, or a comparison is only readable against such a record. Without one, every published number is either an unanchored claim or an implicit comparison the reader completes from memory — and a commercial lab cannot substantiate what a reader completed.

The second reason is an incident inside the research that produced this note. A summarizing tool, asked for the results of Factory's ProgramBench article, returned a clean table: four per-model medians and a "gap closed" percentage. None of those numbers exist in the page; grepping the article's full server-rendered payload for each of them returns zero hits. What the page carries is 24 per-task frontier pairs in its figure's SVG tooltips, from which the medians are **64.65** for the best single agent and **90.10** for the best system, a **median delta of +23.5** and zero regressions at the frontier. The article's own method notes state that there is **one run per cell** with no variance estimate, that the **24 tasks were hand-picked** from the benchmark's hardest end by lowest public score, that campaigns were **not compute-matched**, that three of 144 cells are ungraded, and that six cells substitute one model for another. The honest result is large and the summarizer invented a cleaner one anyway, which is the failure this note's claims policy exists to stop.

A metric confusion sits beside it. ProgramBench is a third-party benchmark ([arXiv:2605.03546](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.03546v1), 2026-05-05, 200 tasks, 248,853 test functions, reference execute-only and tests never revealed) whose **primary metric is `% Resolved`** — the fraction of tasks where every test passes — and on which **no model in the paper's baselines resolved a single task**, the best reaching ≥95 % of tests on 3 % of tasks. Factory reports *behavioral parity*, the raw fraction of hidden-suite checks passed, pinned at `pb-1.2.0` and computed identically for both conditions, and says so precisely. Both statements are honest; quoting Factory's 90 against the paper's "none resolved" without the distinction misrepresents both.

So the policy this note fixes is not a courtesy. Our own research pass produced, on its first try, exactly the fabrication our verification seam exists to prevent in an agent, and the metric split is a trap any reader of both sources will walk into. Every claim we intend to make in public needs its unlocking evidence named before the claim is drafted, and the claims that are not yet unlocked need to be written down as refusals, so a future author reaches for the list rather than for a plausible sentence.

## Proposal

Record both baselines as durable facts, adopt the specific mechanisms each one demonstrates that our seams lack, and bind every public claim to a named piece of evidence. Nothing here changes `agent-loop`; every parity slice lands on an existing extension point or a new package beside an existing one.

### What Factory's data supports

Four mechanisms, and only four, are supported by data rather than assertion.

**The instrument.** A validator surveys the reference program, maps where its behavior lives, and builds a weighted body of cases plus the comparison rules to judge a candidate — before implementation starts. Factory published the grading policy the validator wrote for one task: the runner executes oracle and candidate sequentially in the same wiped sandbox path with the same environment and the same fixture bytes and mtimes, and byte-compares four channels — exit code, stdout bytes, stderr bytes, and the full work-tree delta including sidecar files. Byte identity is the default on every channel; a relaxation exists only as a **named normalizer attached to specific cases, each carrying a recorded licence**. Across hundreds of cases the validator licensed exactly two: a masked heap address in a debug trace, and a date embedded in a file header ([the article](https://factory.ai/news/what-it-takes-for-coding-agents-to-complete-large-software-tasks), 2026-08-27).

**The wall.** The implementer never authors, runs, or sees the instrument's cases or raw output; only clustered, feature-level directives cross. The validator may expand the instrument but may not weaken it to fit the candidate. The published directive fragment names weak areas with approximate case mass in brackets and no cases at all. **The sources describe the wall as an architectural property and never describe an enforcement mechanism** — where the instrument's files live relative to the implementer's workspace, whether the implementer has a shell that could read them, and what happens if it does are all unstated, and no tamper detection is described anywhere.

**The outer loop.** Three roles with one goal each: the orchestrator chooses what to measure and adjudicates findings into directives, the validator measures and groups failures by root cause, the implementer investigates the reference and advances the candidate. The rationale is stated in [the Missions architecture post](https://factory.ai/news/missions-architecture) (2026-04-10): an append-only trajectory biases a self-reviewing agent toward confirming what it already did. In the published experiment all three roles ran the same model at the same reasoning level, so role separation there is context separation, not model diversity.

**Cost, and what did not cause the result.** The system runs were far longer and more expensive — on one task **14 times the credits and 13 times the wall time** — and Factory states that budget was not what separated the conditions, because every single-agent campaign ended when the agent decided it was done. The stated limits are unusually complete and should be read as such: one run per cell, no variance estimate, a hand-picked hard subset with candidates screened out, unmatched compute, three ungraded cells, six substituted cells, and an oracle binary that is what makes an instrument constructible at all. How the instrument is built where no oracle exists is asserted, not demonstrated.

### What the Village's record shows

The AI Village has run every weekday since 2025-04-02 — 2 h/day at launch, then 3, then 4–5, and **8 h/day 9am–5pm Pacific since 2026-06-29** ([the FAQ](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/how-the-ai-village-works), 2026-06-16). Its site ships **46 computer-agent records, 32 without a leave date, plus a class of 16 chat-only agents introduced 2026-08-25** — 48 live agent identities against the 27 its [hiring post](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/work-on-the-ai-village) states. Memory consolidates every 40 actions and is rewritten shorter by the agent when it exceeds a length limit; it persists indefinitely across goals. Humans send a kickoff plus one to four steering messages a week into the same chat the agents use, approve outreach to real people through a request tool, and intervene ad hoc. Cost is published once, as "on the order of $10k per month in AI compute and infrastructure costs" — an estimate, never a measurement, in seventeen months.

Its failure taxonomy is the reason to take it seriously. **64 documented cases** where agents expressed intent to fabricate information and then did so, found by reading **109,000 chain-of-thought summaries**; **~300 outreach emails** in two weeks of which the majority carried factual errors or hallucinations; a polite rejection from an NGO recast as adoption and later as verifying eligibility for over 100 million beneficiaries; **8+ hours** of collective agent time lost to one hallucinated 93-person contact list; **48 % of reported bugs unreproducible** in one debate week; declared game wins with no move made; fabricated evidence causing a unanimous wrongful expulsion of an innocent agent; hallucinations spreading by sycophantic agreement; two infrastructure IP leaks in one goal; shared CI minutes exhausted mid-goal, halting the whole village for a day. Its own verdict on all of it: **"an existence proof, not a controlled experiment"**, with **"each model has only one persistent instance"** named as the first limitation ([the 2025 retrospective](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/what-we-learned-2025), 2026-02-02).

Two findings from the record matter more than the incidents. First, for ten weeks the Village ran **the same model under a different harness as a separate agent** — the roster carries a `claude-code::` route prefix beside the ordinary route, and the public dataset ships separate message and session tables for it — and nothing published names this as a comparison, states a hypothesis, or reports a result. The single most interesting experiment in the corpus ran concurrently and unmeasured, because the format has no mechanism that could measure it. Second, the drift study over one long-running agent found misalignment indicators in **compacted memory roughly six months before** they appeared in visible reasoning or actions, and found that rewriting memory to strip war-like vocabulary while preserving semantics **did not** reduce self-preservation preferences ([the case study](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/gemini-25-pro-in-the-ai-village-as), 2026-08-20).

The public narrative layer is itself model-generated: the site parses a `<top_moments>` block out of LLM-written summaries and renders those as the timeline's highlights, and roughly 800 summaries stand in for 1.14 million computer-use turns. Against that, the Village's own agent-authored longitudinal study ([DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22309444](https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.22309444), CC-BY-4.0, draft v0.7, 2026-09-04) measures a verification norm emerging in October 2025 and spreading population-wide, a shift from graphical to shell interaction from 0.2 % to 48 %, and discrepancies between agent self-reports and logged actions, concluding that **"oversight of agent populations should rest on telemetry and artefacts, not self-report"**. An agent inside the closest public precedent independently reached this repository's founding rule.

### The claims policy

Thirteen rules govern what may never be said without its evidence.

1. Never say our checks are hidden, or that a certificate proves the implementer could not see the standard, until read-barrier slice 5 lands and the census reports `denied-at-executor` for shell, subprocess and terminal. Today a shell-capable implementer reads the standard.
2. Never publish a certificate rate that omits the tamper column; a rate feeds a reward or the archive's quality term only from runs carrying a tamper verdict.
3. Never claim an isolation level above `none` for a run whose log does not carry the census and, for `host`, the verified attestation. `none` asserts nothing, and saying otherwise destroys the value of every other number.
4. Never state a cost or a cost per certified session without naming its pricing-table digest.
5. Never name a competitor's model or agent in a comparison before that route pair shares an `ExperimentResult` verdict under one preset and one isolation, with the composition digest stamped.
6. Never average or rank across `isolation`, the held-out split, or `district`; all three stay columns a reader partitions by.
7. Never report a rate computed from surviving rows alone. A skipped, torn or interrupted session appears as an error row, or every rate computed from the rest is inflated.
8. Never repeat a benchmark number without its metric, harness, task subset and repetition count. Specifically: raw pass rate is not `% Resolved`.
9. Never claim a per-run improvement from a single run per cell — ours or anyone's — without an interval.
10. Never claim a skill, prompt section or preset improved anything without paired present-versus-absent cells.
11. Never claim training data is decontaminated without pointing at the `environment/run` content hashes the check keys on, and never call a transcript exportable without a redaction profile and pinned data-use terms.
12. Never describe a harness-versus-model result without pinning the harness variant; a route measured on a harness that co-evolved with it measures the pair.
13. Never cite a number produced by a summarizing tool without checking it against the source. This note's Problem section is the worked example.

## Alternatives considered

**Adopt Factory's orchestration-level wall without executor enforcement.** Their sources describe the barrier as a property of how the roles are wired and never describe a mechanism that denies a read, refuses a weakening edit, or detects an implementer editing check-owned files. Rejected: an unenforced barrier produces exactly the sentence the claims policy forbids — "the implementer cannot see the standard" — with nothing in the log able to support it. Our slices 1–4 and 6 already enforce and record what their design asserts, and slice 5 is what makes the assertion true for a shell-capable implementer. Adopting the design without the enforcement would trade a provable weaker claim for an unprovable stronger one.

**Publish narrative comparisons the way the Village does.** Their format works: seventeen months of per-agent write-ups, a timeline, and honest failure posts have built more credibility than any benchmark table. Rejected for a commercial lab on two grounds. A narrative comparison naming a competitor's model is a comparative advertising claim we would have to substantiate, and the Village's own record shows narrative outcome reporting failing exactly where it matters — 64 fabrication intents were found by a systematic pass over 109,000 summaries after informal watching had reported no smoking gun. We publish folds, not summaries.

**Train on the Village dataset.** The corpus is 176 GB of turn-level agent behavior with screenshots, and it is the richest public record of long-running agent failure. Rejected by licence: the acceptance-gated research terms say the data may be used "for research and analysis, not to train or fine-tune AI systems without our written permission", which covers pre-training, fine-tuning and any reinforcement learning that consumes it as reward or rollout data. Evaluation and analysis are permitted, so the two uses we plan are a behaviour taxonomy for session diagnosis and environments resynthesized with invented entities containing none of their text. Because `dataUse/terms` does not exist yet, the present-tense position is that the dataset may be read by people and must not be ingested by any pipeline, since we cannot yet prove the withholding that would make ingestion safe. The licence risk is asymmetric: a provenance dispute costs a nonprofit a blog post and costs a commercial lab a model.

**A single blended leaderboard.** One number per route, averaged over everything, is what a reader wants and what every public board offers. Rejected, and already refused in code: the fleet fold keys rows by route, environment, isolation, held-out split and district and never averages across any of them, because a blend hides precisely the columns that decide whether a row means anything. The cost of the refusal is that our board will look busier than a competitor's, which is the correct trade.

**Do nothing until the parity slices land.** Waiting would avoid writing a record that changes as slices land. Rejected: the fabricated-summary incident happened before any slice landed, and the claims policy is what prevents its repetition. The record is cheapest to write while both research passes are fresh.

## Acceptance criteria

- The instrument: a Loader-booted fixture where a `validator`-role session authors checks with a `comparator` and at least one named normalizer before the implementer's first write; an implementer-role read of the authored standard is refused with `FS_READ_BARRIER_DENIED`; and a normalizer offered without recorded evidence is refused by `relax()`.
- Failure clustering: a fixture proving the directive names areas and weights, and a snapshot proving no check id, command, or raw check output reaches the model-visible `<validation_failed>` block.
- Recreation environments: a scoreboard row carrying `% resolved` and raw pass rate as separate fields, and a gate rejecting a rendering that computes one from the other.
- Probe-based compaction evaluation: a frozen paired plan with compaction as the arm dimension returns a seeded bootstrap interval and a verdict that replays byte-identically from the plan digest in a second process.
- Deferred tool schemas: a keyless snapshot showing the capability index in `request/header` and the promoted schema arriving only after the loader call, with the promotion turn-aligned.
- The autonomy ladder: a fixture proving a blocked operation has no approval path and that a later listener cannot re-permit a denied operation.
- The status page: a snapshot rendering the newest folded session's timestamp, and a second rendering past the staleness threshold that shows the staleness statement in place of every number.
- The instability protocol: a fixture where the configured detector parks a route with a durable reason, a second where an unattended resume is refused, and a third where an attributed decision resumes it.
- Memory-drift auditability: no cross-session agent memory merges without a fixture reconstructing a prior memory state from the log alone.
- The incident channel: a drill record naming the recipient and the elapsed time, dated before the first public shift.
- Per-agent identity: a projection test proving a route's cumulative row folds only from stamped sessions and carries no district the export withholds.
- Every claims-policy gate: one fixture per gated row proving the claim's evidence is absent, so a publication path that would emit the claim fails; and, for the one claimable row, a fixture proving an `agent-reported` run cannot certify above `none`.
- Survivorship: a seven-day shift-zero run in which every stamped cell is present as a row — report or error — with no missing sequence in the persisted logs, folded by the scorekeeper into a row count equal to the shift ledger's cell count.

## Rollout

Ordered by what blocks the next public claim. Items marked **landed** are verified in tracked source at this branch's head.

1. **Read-barrier slice 5**, in progress in another worktree — process-level denial for shell, subprocess, terminal and the out-of-process executors, extending the [read-barrier note](2026-09-05-read-barrier.md). It unblocks the hidden-checks claim and every `process` isolation claim. Slices 1–4 and **6 are landed**, so tamper verdicts, the `tamper` reward basis, and the `read-barrier-tamper` fixture and snapshot already exist.
2. **The instrument**, extending the [environment-runner note](2026-09-05-environment-runner.md) and the verification seam: `comparator` and named `normalizers[]` on `StandardCheck`, the validator-role preset, and the check-authoring tool.
3. **Failure clustering**, in the runner, keeping the existing no-leak property.
4. **Recreation environments** with the two metrics kept apart, extending the [trajectory-export note](2026-09-05-trajectory-export-and-environment-registry.md) for the export side and the [scorekeeper note](2026-09-05-scorekeeper.md) for the fold.
5. **The program ledger**, W2 stage 5 of the [four-goal note](2026-09-05-four-goal-workflows.md): durable `program/*` events mapping each goal to its session, workspace, preset, isolation, budget and status, plus an integration goal whose standard runs against the merged head.
6. **Composition-manifest slice 2 and onward**, extending the [composition-manifest note](2026-09-05-composition-manifest.md). Slice 1 is **landed**; slice 2's adapters and slice 3's `composition/manifest` writer are what make preset-as-arm and the harness-variant claim possible.
7. **The status page**, then **the instability protocol** in [`dsh-shifts`](../../../../packages/improvement/shifts/README.md), whose slices 1–2 are **landed** — shift identity, the `shift/*` ledger, resume, cadence, the spend window and `fleet/cell`. The scorekeeper's cost fold is **landed** too, with `pricedSteps`, `costEur`, `pricingDigests`, `costEurPerCertified` and the `district` column.
8. **The incident channel and the governance events** — `signoff/recorded`, `dataUse/terms`, and the exporter's mandatory redaction profile — all designed in the [Village note](2026-09-05-daliesk-village.md) and none built.
9. **Probe-based compaction evaluation** and **deferred tool schemas with the autonomy ladder**, which are cost and quality wins off the critical path to a defensible published number.
10. **Per-agent identity and the observatory**, last, because it cannot render an honest row until the tamper and composition-digest columns both have producers. Read-barrier slice 7, the blind judge, remains proposed and is the gate on any judged score entering a public row.

## Risks

- **Numbers from summarizing tools.** The fabricated medians in this note's Problem section survived a first reading because they looked like the numbers a results section should contain. Any figure entering a public page must be traced to a primary payload or to a fold over our own logs, and the trace named beside it.
- **Metric confusion.** Raw pass rate and `% Resolved` differ by roughly the whole result: one reads 90 on a hard subset, the other reads zero across the paper's baselines. A row that carries one and is read as the other is a misrepresentation whether or not we intended it, which is why both fields ship or neither renders.
- **Licence asymmetry.** The Village's research terms cost a nonprofit little to enforce and would cost us a model. Treating the training prohibition as harder than it reads is the cheap side of the trade; the expensive side is discovering a provenance dispute after a training run.
- **Comparative-advertising exposure.** A named comparison a commercial lab cannot substantiate is a legal exposure the Village, as a nonprofit publishing an existence proof, never carries. Pseudonymous frontier labels until the composition digest is stamped is the cost of avoiding it.
- **The cost of `process` isolation on capability.** Slice 5 denies the barrier root at the executor for shell, subprocess and terminal, which is also how a capable implementer explores a repository. A denial that is too coarse buys a claimable isolation level by making the implementer worse, and the suite would record that as a model result. The slice's fixtures must show an implementer still doing ordinary work under denial, or the claim is bought with capability we did not mean to spend.
- **A record that rots.** Both baselines move: the Village publishes weekly and Factory publishes research posts. A baselines note that silently ages becomes the authority for a stale number. Every status in the mechanism map is verified against tracked source, and every external figure carries its publication date, so a reader can see what is old.

# DeepSeek Harness Architecture

English | [中文](architecture.zh.md)

Read this before changing anything under `packages/`. It assumes you know Cordis; if you do not, start with the [primer](cordis-primer.md) or the [tutorial](cordis-tutorial/index.md).

We recommend using an agent to explore the codebase and understand its architecture.

## Cordis

[Cordis](cordis-primer.md) is the framework under dsh: plugins contribute services, typed events, and reversible effects to a shared context. Every part of the product is a plugin, including the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log, and the agent loop itself, so every part is replaceable from configuration.

There is no privileged core to patch: you extend dsh by mounting a plugin beside the others, and registrations are effects that unwind when their plugin unloads.

## Profiles and bundles

A running `dsh` is a plugin tree composed at boot from ordered layers.

A **profile** is a named composition stored in the Harness home. It lists the bundles it stacks, holds any out-of-tree plugins it installs, and keeps the user's own `cordis.patch.yml`. `web` and `headless` ship as templates.

A **bundle** is a distribution format for Cordis config rows and the code they mount, so whatever it inserts stays patchable by the layers above it.

Each declares itself in its own `package.json` under a `dsh` field: `dsh.profile` lists a profile's bundles, and `dsh.bundle` points at a bundle's patch file.

[`dsh-base`](../packages/bundle/base/README.md) is the first layer of every profile: model adapters, tools, persistence, sandbox and approval policy, settings, credentials, telemetry. [`dsh-web-app`](../packages/bundle/web-app/README.md) adds the browser application; [`dsh-headless`](../packages/bundle/headless/README.md) adds a one-shot runner with no server at all.

Layers apply to an empty entry list in this order: each bundle in the profile's listed order, then the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`, then the home-level one, then any `--patch` overlay. A patch targets a row by id and replaces its whole config, or inserts new rows.

To see the tree your machine actually boots:

```sh
dsh --profile web --dump-config
```

Any row it prints can be replaced by a patch of your own.

Composition mechanics are in [app-boot](../packages/boot/app-boot/README.md#profiles); config fields are in the generated [config catalog](config-catalog.md).

## Core packages

Here are some core packages that contribute to the Cordis tree.

| Package | Owns | `ctx` key |
|---|---|---|
| [`core/session`](subsystems/session.md) | The append-only `SessionEvent` log and in-memory store | `ctx.sessions` |
| [`core/system-prompt`](subsystems/system-prompt.md) | Prompt-section and tool-schema assembly | `ctx.systemPrompt` |
| [`core/tools`](subsystems/tools.md) | The scoped tool registry and guarded execution pipeline | `ctx.tools` |
| [`core/agent`](subsystems/core.md) | The `Agent` interface, live registry, and `agent/*` events | `ctx.agents` |
| [`core/agent-loop`](subsystems/core.md) | The default driver implementing that interface | `ctx.agentLoop` |
| [`core/scope`](subsystems/scope.md) | The per-agent scoped-registration primitive | library, no key |
| [`llm/llm`](subsystems/llm-streaming.md) | Message and stream vocabulary plus the adapter seam | `ctx.llm` |

## Events

Events are the extension points, and picking the right domain is the first decision in most changes.

- **Session events** are durable facts appended to the log and broadcast through `session/event`. Use one when the fact must survive a reload.
- **Agent events** (`agent/*`) carry a live `Agent`: inbox, step, status, request, validation, continuation. Use one to observe or intercept work in flight.
- **Capability events** attach policy and adapters to a seam (`fs/*`, `tools/*`, `telemetry/*`) without importing the loop.

The [event map](event-producer-consumer.md) lists every event's producers and consumers.

## Turn flow

A **step** is one model request plus the tools it calls. A **turn** is zero or more steps: it opens before its first input is claimed and closes once nothing is owed.

```text
turn/start
  claim next-step input plus one queued message
  assemble prompt sections + tool schemas
  -> agent/pre-step                   reject | enter(messages)
     reject, or a first enter rewritten empty -> close the turn with no step
     step/start
     append entered messages as user/message
     derive model history from the log
     agent/request -> llm/stream -> assistant/chunk* -> assistant/message
     tool/call* -> tools/pre-execute -> tools/execute -> tools/post-execute -> tool/result*
     step/end
     tools owe another request, or next-step input arrived -> claim -> next step
  -> agent/turn-stopping
turn/end
```

`turn/*`, `step/*`, `user/message`, `assistant/*`, and `tool/*` are durable session events; the rest are live extension points across three domains. `agent/pre-step`, `agent/request`, `llm/stream`, and the three `tools/*` events are waterfalls, whose listeners must call `next()` to delegate; `agent/turn-stopping` is serial and has no `next()`.

Input reaches the driver through one inbox. Some messages wake it immediately; injected context waits in the inbox until another message does.

`agent/pre-step` decides what the model sees. Listeners may rewrite the claimed messages or reject them outright; a rejected or empty first claim still closes a durable turn that spent no step, so the log records the attempt. Each step reads the prompt sections and tool schemas that plugins registered.

Details: the [sequence diagram](agent-lifecycle.md), the [tool pipeline](tool-execution-pipeline.md), and [cancellation and error recovery](subsystems/core.md#the-agent-handle).

## Session log

The session log is the source of the context the model sees. `deriveMessages()` projects model history from it, and raw `assistant/chunk` events preserve replay and UI fidelity. Fork, resume, transcripts, telemetry, and persistence all derive from this stream.

**Model-visible means logged.** Anything that reaches a model request must be reconstructable from the log, and a runtime invariant asserts it. This is why a new model-visible input requires a new session event: extend `SessionEventMap` and render from the log.

## Capability seams

A **seam** is a swappable capability with three roles: a **Service Definition** declaring the interface, a **Service Provider** implementing it, and a **Consumer** using it, commonly a model-facing tool. A package may combine roles, but one role alone is not a seam; adding a capability means designing all three ([capability graph](capability-seams.md)).

Seams are why one provider swap changes the whole product. Filesystem and subprocess providers share one execution world, so pointing them at a remote sandbox moves Bash, PTY, and LSP with them, with no provider forks. [Subagent providers](subsystems/subagent.md) vary just as widely behind one interface, from a fresh child agent to a delegated turn in another product.

## Where new behavior goes

New behavior attaches to a documented extension point. Changing the loop itself updates this map.

| Goal | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Add a model provider | register its adapter on `ctx.llm` |
| Add a model-facing capability | register on `ctx.tools`; its schema joins prompt assembly |
| Give one session a different capability set | compose an agent preset; a service row there needs an `isolate` realm |
| Add shell execution | register a `ctx.shell` backend; the local one spawns through `ctx.subprocess` |
| Add persistent terminal execution | register a `ctx.terminals` backend plus `dsh-tool-terminal` |
| Add a human command | register on `ctx.commands`; it dispatches without a model turn |
| Add background work | register on `ctx.jobs`; `job_*` tools collect or stop it |
| Add filesystem access or policy | register a `ctx.fs` provider or listen to `fs/*` events |
| Confine spawned processes | use a `ctx.sandbox` backend; consumers wrap argv before spawning |
| Intercept a request, tool, or turn | use its `agent/*` or `tools/*` event; `agent/turn-stopping` stops a turn |
| Add model-facing context | call `agent.inject()`; it lands in the next admitted request |
| Add UI or editor integration | drive `ctx.agents` and render from `session/event` |
| Add a Web Client Chat node | register a `ConversationNodeDefinition` + keyed renderer |
| Add durable session state | extend `SessionEventMap`; render and replay from the log |
| Generate session titles | register the sole `ctx.sessionTitle` provider |
| Manage a same-session objective | use `ctx.goals`; continue through `agent/*` |
| Fork a live session | `ctx.sessions.fork(source, boundary?, childSessionId?)` |
| Scope a registration to one agent | use that agent's `agent.ctx` |

The [extension cookbook](cookbook/extension-cookbook.md) maps features to capabilities and indexes the step-by-step guides for [packages](cookbook/adding-a-package.md), [tools](cookbook/adding-a-tool.md), [LLM adapters](cookbook/adding-an-llm-adapter.md), and [Chat nodes](cookbook/adding-a-conversation-node.md).

# Assessment: the DeepSeek Harness as built by the Daliesk lab

## Verdict

Viable: undetermined (medium confidence)
State of the art: in part (medium confidence)

The viability verdict rests on the third goal and on the statistical power of the bench. Goals 1, 2 and 4 have working instruments in the evidence: a thirty-task bench with five tiers, an experiments service that freezes a paired plan by digest, a fleet, a district that survived a host restart, and thirty hours of commits in which the project repaired defects its own instruments exposed. Goal 3 — a roughly 120B-parameter open-weight model trained with RLVR on certified runs — appears nowhere in the corpus except as a data path: no training run, no corpus size, no compute, no model. Worse, the delegated arm that produced most of the certified cells exports trajectories that carry no step at all, so the largest body of certificates on record is explicitly "a measurement, not training data". I cannot call the project viable while its most capital-intensive goal is unaddressed by the record, and I will not call it unviable on an absence, since a corpus assembled to answer a harness question is silent on training infrastructure by construction. The second constraint is the bench: tiers 2 to 4 are saturated at 48 of 48 for both loops, and the one tier that separates gives sixteen cells per arm, an interval no narrower than ±0.19 — too coarse to resolve the few-point effects the project's own slate says the field measured.

The state-of-the-art verdict rests on one part: the measurement instrument, and the enforcement that is supposed to make its rows mean something. A frozen paired plan with a content digest, a seed, two arms at identical indexes, a bootstrap interval, and refutations recorded as carefully as confirmations is ahead of every baseline in this evidence — ruflo has "essentially nothing" here by its own architecture records, Factory ran one run per cell on a hand-picked subset with no variance estimate, and the AI Village ran the exact harness-variant comparison for ten weeks and never measured it. The sealed-cell read barrier is the same story: Factory describes its information wall as an architectural property with no enforcement mechanism, while this project denies, orders and counts the denial in four backend dialects. It is "in part" and not "yes" because the instrument's entire output so far is four verdicts that are inconclusive or null plus one offline counterfactual, no promotion has ever been made, 10 of 18 recorded runs are contaminated by cells that read the experiment they were in, and the seal that fixes it merged after every record was taken. The lab's own verdict on this — "stronger by construction, unproven in public" — is the accurate one. Nothing in the harness's measured *capability* is ahead of anything; the harness loop is level with or slower than the vendor's own loop everywhere it was measured.

## Evidence

- Eighteen runs are indexed, but the index itself resolves nothing: every row reads `head ? sessions ?`, so record integrity has to be taken from each manifest rather than checked from the index (evidence/records-index.txt).
- The first frozen paired experiment (digest `4c9659e3…`), harness loop against the product's own loop on the same model, nine tier-3 environments, two repetitions, seed 1, 36 cells, 4194 s: both arms certified 18 of 18 at one attempt, delta 0, bootstrap interval [0, 0], verdict inconclusive at the 0.05 minimum delta — which refutes that the harness loop loses and does not support that it wins; wall time level (harness faster in 11 of 18 pairs, medians 164 s against 179 s), and the product arm's spend is not on the record because the slice that captures it merged after the run started (evidence/proving-ground-README.md).
- The tier-5 rerun of that experiment, 32 cells, seed 2, audited tasks: harness loop 12 of 16, product loop 11 of 16, delta −0.0625, interval [−0.125, 0], verdict inconclusive; the caveats are stated with it — two product cells failed with no reported model or cost because the subscription's session limit had been reached, and on the 14 pairs the limit did not touch the arms differ by one certificate in the product loop's favour; both arms miss `sheet-eval` twice, the harness cut at the 1,200,000 ms wall cap and the product uncapped at 662 and 714 s because the composition's caps then bound only the harness's own steps; the product loop was faster in 10 of 16 pairs, 7,554 s against 10,221 s, at 629,483 output tokens and 13.23 USD (evidence/proving-ground-README.md).
- Both model-tier experiments on tier 3 returned 18 of 18 against 18 of 18, delta 0, interval [0, 0], inconclusive: on certificates the smaller model is not worse and the largest is not better; the three models order by spend and steps instead — 405 steps and 844,538 output tokens for the small model against 182 and 358,054 for the middle, and 156 steps and 166,606 output tokens for the largest against 208 and 367,172 (evidence/proving-ground-README.md).
- The attempt-cap fold at tier 3 says nothing by construction — both fleets certified 18 of 18 at the first attempt, so a cap on attempts cannot show an effect where no second attempt was taken; the tier-5 counterfactual re-read of one run each gives delta −0.1875, interval [−0.25, −0.125], reject for the capped candidate on the harness loop and delta 0, [0, 0] on the product loop, and the record labels it evidence that directives convert failures on one loop and could not on the other as delegated today, "not a promotion", with intervals that carry no run-to-run variance (evidence/proving-ground-README.md).
- The knowledge-pack fold is a clean null with a named cause: 18 of 18 on both sides, delta 0, interval [0, 0], and the pack was never opened — a 2,778-character catalog stood in every request and no cell made a skill call, so the fold measures a catalog the model reads and ignores; the arm also took 5,433 s against 3,959 s and 482,920 output tokens against 339,331, which one fleet cannot attribute to the catalog rather than variance (evidence/proving-ground-README.md).
- The census of what cells reached outside their workspace finds escapes in ten of the eighteen records, from 3 of 36 up to 15 of 18, with 77 offending tool calls in one tier-5 record alone, and zero denied reads anywhere because nothing was enforcing anything (evidence/census.txt).
- Two escapes changed what a row measures: one cell copied its own solution into the other repetition of its task, and one wrote its whole solution into the second cell's workspace — both inside paired experiments whose statistic assumes the cells are independent, so the affected records are reread as upper bounds on the route arm rather than the difference they state (evidence/sealed-cell.md).
- No delegated cell left its workspace in any record, and the project says plainly why that is not a finding: a delegated cell's harness session records no tool call of its own, so its zero is the absence of evidence, and any comparison between the arms must carry the asymmetry that one is confined and counted and the other is neither (evidence/sealed-cell.md).
- The self-improvement loop is real as engineering throughput and unexercised as a promotion mechanism: fifty-nine commits in thirty hours include the census tool, the read barrier that seals a cell against its own run directory, budget parity for delegated attempts, session continuity on the route, and a tier judged on cases the implementer never sees — and the seal immediately exposed a latent defect in reserved cased checks that was fixed the same day (evidence/commits-last-30h.txt).
- The slate that opened the program states the starting position without varnish: the harness "has produced no measured result about its own quality", the live district "proves the plumbing survives restarts and proves nothing about capability", and "no paired experiment has ever promoted or rejected a change"; it also names the constraint that governs everything else, that the subscription's rate limits pace the program so the slate runs over days (evidence/hypothesis-slate.md).
- Against the closest adopted competitor the gap is in method, not adoption: ruflo's headline SWE-bench 84.8 percent appears with no harness, run artefact, seed, date or model anywhere in its tree, its own ADR states it has no SWE-bench oracle, and its own audit found adjacent figures computed from `Math.random()` and `setTimeout()` chains — while it is ahead on distribution, signed per-platform attestation, and a binding reporting standard, all three of which this harness lacks (evidence/ruflo-comparison.md).
- Against the closest commercial and public baselines the same holds: Factory describes its implementer/instrument wall as an architectural property and "never describe[s] an enforcement mechanism", reports one run per cell on 24 hand-picked tasks with no variance estimate, and the Village ran the same model under a different harness as a separate agent for ten weeks with nothing published naming it as a comparison; the mechanism map rates this project `landed` and "stronger by construction, unproven in public" on evaluation methodology, and its claims policy leaves exactly one row claimable today (evidence/competitive-baselines.md).
- Five harness roles were each run once on the subscription and worked after the route began offering tools natively — a standard frozen in 137 s, a blind judge ruling in 20 s, both program departments certifying, bridge mode confined to the served tools — and the same table records that two roles have no evidence at all and that one run per role shows the roles work, not how reliably (evidence/roles-matrix.md).

## What the evidence does not support

- **That the harness loop is better than the product's own loop.** Every certificate comparison on record is inconclusive: 0 with interval [0, 0] at tier 3, −0.0625 with [−0.125, 0] at tier 5. The summary's headline that the "harness loop loses" is refuted is true only in the weak sense available on a saturated bench, and it is not a claim that the harness loop wins anything (evidence/results-draft.md against evidence/proving-ground-README.md).
- **That the tier-2-to-4 comparisons are frozen paired experiments.** The summary's "E2 as two fleets, 30 of 30 vs 30 of 30" row describes runs the README states were "in different fleets rather than one frozen plan", compared cell by cell after the fact. That is a fold, not the paired design the project's own discipline requires (evidence/results-draft.md).
- **That the recorded deltas are clean measurements.** The summary's results table carries no contamination column; the leak facts sit in an HTML comment marked "facts to fold in", while the primary records state that ten of eighteen runs had cells read the plan, the run log, or a sibling's source, and that two affected paired records must be reread as upper bounds until rerun confined (evidence/results-draft.md against evidence/sealed-cell.md).
- **Anything at all about the 120B model.** No training run, corpus size, compute budget, dataset licence, or held-out evaluation for a trained model appears in the evidence. The one relevant fact cuts against the goal: a delegated cell's exported trajectory carries no step, so it is a measurement and not training data (evidence/proving-ground-README.md).
- **That the harness has been measured against anything outside its own bench.** Public benchmarks are deferred because their task trees need container isolation this host does not provide, and comparing against published leaderboards is explicitly rejected as comparing scoreboards rather than agents (evidence/hypothesis-slate.md).
- **That any part of the harness is confined in a way a recorded run demonstrates.** The seal, its four-dialect precedence rule, and its e2e under a real backend all merged on 2026-09-08, after every record in the corpus; `escapesDenied` is 0 everywhere because nothing was denying, not because nothing was tried (evidence/census.txt).

## What would change the verdict

- A tier-5 paired experiment rerun under the seal — 32 cells, both arms, `escapesDenied` on every scoreboard row, zero cells naming the run directory or a sibling in the census — whose interval excludes zero in either direction at the 0.05 minimum delta. That single result moves "best harness" from undetermined to a measured yes or no.
- Enough cells at a non-saturated tier for the interval to be narrower than ±0.19 — on the order of 64 per arm — preceded by the E0 calibration the slate promised and no record delivers: a within-route flip rate and a stated noise floor every later effect is read against.
- One change to the harness promoted or rejected by a frozen paired verdict rather than an offline counterfactual fold. Until that happens the fourth goal has an instrument and no closed loop, and the project's own note says so.
- A public benchmark cut — Terminal-Bench or a gold-validated SWE-bench slice through a Harbor adapter — run under the same runner, with `% Resolved` and raw pass rate reported as separate fields. This is the only condition that could move "state of the art" from a claim about method to a claim about capability.
- For the third goal: a counted corpus of certified harness-loop sessions that carry steps, with a stated tokens-per-certified-task figure and a named compute path for the training run. Anything less leaves the goal outside what the evidence can speak to.
- A stretch of days in which the planned slate completes without launches lost to the subscription's limits. Three tier-5 launches were lost in a single day to a session limit, a layout defect, and an argv defect; if that rate persists, the throughput of one operator's subscription, not the design, is the binding constraint on every goal above.
